summary.text: Take \(n=18\): since \(\sigma(18)=39\), its reduced abundancy denominator is \(a(18)=18/\gcd(18,39)=6\). Now \(\sigma(6)=12\), so \(a(6)=1\), a power of two, meaning \(a(18)=6\) belongs to A005153, whereas \(18\) does not because \(a(18)=6\) is not a power of two.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d
\]
denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(n\). The sum of the reciprocals of the positive divisors of \(n\) is
\[
\sum_{d\mid n}\frac1d=\frac{\sigma(n)}n.
\]
Indeed, the map \(d\mapsto n/d\) permutes the positive divisors of \(n\), so
\[
\sum_{d\mid n}\frac1d
 =\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}\frac nd
 =\frac1n\sum_{e\mid n}e
 =\frac{\sigma(n)}n.
\]
Consequently, if \(a(n)\) denotes the denominator of this rational number in lowest terms, then for every positive \(n\),
\[
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,\sigma(n))}.
\]

In the stated interpretation of A005153, a positive integer \(m\) belongs to A005153 precisely when \(a(m)\) is a power of two; that is, when there is a nonnegative integer \(k\) such that
\[
a(m)=2^k.
\]
We disprove the conjectured implication
\[
a(n)\in\mathrm{A005153}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\in\mathrm{A005153}
\]
by taking \(n=18\).

First compute \(a(18)\). The positive divisors of \(18\) are
\[
1,2,3,6,9,18,
\]
and hence
\[
\sigma(18)=1+2+3+6+9+18=39.
\]
Since
\[
\gcd(18,39)=3,
\]
we obtain
\[
a(18)=\frac{18}{\gcd(18,39)}=\frac{18}{3}=6.
\]
Equivalently, the reciprocal-divisor sum is
\[
\sum_{d\mid18}\frac1d=\frac{39}{18}=\frac{13}{6},
\]
whose reduced denominator is indeed \(6\).

We next show that the premise of the conjecture holds for \(n=18\), namely that \(a(18)=6\) belongs to A005153. For this, calculate \(a(6)\). The positive divisors of \(6\) are
\[
1,2,3,6,
\]
so
\[
\sigma(6)=1+2+3+6=12.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(6)=\frac{6}{\gcd(6,12)}=\frac66=1.
\]
The number \(1\) is a power of two, since \(1=2^0\). By the defining membership condition for A005153, this proves
\[
6\in\mathrm{A005153}.
\]
As \(a(18)=6\), it follows that
\[
a(18)\in\mathrm{A005153}.
\]
Thus the premise of the proposed implication is true at \(n=18\).

It remains to show that its conclusion is false there. If \(18\) belonged to A005153, then its denominator \(a(18)=6\) would have to be a power of two. But \(6\) is not a power of two. To see this rigorously, suppose that \(6=2^k\) for some nonnegative integer \(k\). Since \(3\mid6\), this would give \(3\mid2^k\). Because \(3\) is prime, a prime dividing a power must divide its base, so this would imply \(3\mid2\), which is impossible. Hence there is no \(k\ge0\) with \(6=2^k\). It follows that
\[
18\notin\mathrm{A005153}.
\]

We have therefore exhibited the concrete counterexample
\[
n=18,
\]
for which
\[
a(18)=6\in\mathrm{A005153}
\qquad\text{but}\qquad
18\notin\mathrm{A005153}.
\]
Hence it is false that, for every \(n\), membership of \(a(n)\) in A005153 implies membership of \(n\) in A005153.
